concepts.def: The next best thing you gave up
Giving up one thing to get another
What you gain from the choice

walkthroughs.body_html:
Opportunity cost = the next best thing you didn't pick.

Spend £10 on pizza → opportunity cost is the cinema ticket you didn't buy. 🍕

Examples:

  • Study or watch TV?
  • Save or spend?
  • Eco-friendly bag or cheap bag?
  • Government: more nurses or more police?

Each is a trade-off.

To make good choices, compare:

  • Benefit — what do I gain?
  • Cost — what do I give up?

If benefit > cost, it's usually a smart choice. ⚖️

mcqs.q: Is a trade deficit necessarily bad?
options: Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
A trade deficit means a country has no factories.
Not necessarily — it can reflect strong domestic demand, attractive investment opportunities, or borrowing to fund growth. Context matters more than the headline figure.
A trade deficit always means a country is losing wealth and failing economically.

mcqs.q: What causes the supply curve to shift?
options: Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
Changes in production costs, technology, taxes/subsidies, number of producers, expectations — anything affecting supply other than the good's own price.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
When demand rises, the supply curve shifts right to meet it.

mcqs.q: What is the principle of comparative advantage?
options: Countries should specialise in producing goods with lower opportunity cost relative to others — even a country worse at everything still has a comparative advantage in something.
Comparative advantage means richer countries should help poorer ones.
Supply shifts only when consumers want more.
A country should produce whatever it can make best.
